claim: DNA base-base mismatches are generated by nucleotide misincorporation during DNA synthesis, meiotic recombination, somatic recombination between nearly identical repeats, or chemical modification such as hydrolytic deamination of cytosine.
source: DNA base-base mismatches are generated by nucleotide misincorporation during DNA synthesis, meiotic recombination, somatic recombination between nearly identical repeats, or chemical modification such as hydrolytic deamination of cytosine (Li, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li, 2008

claim: DNA mismatches are introduced intentionally in some genome editing approaches.
source: They are also introduced intentionally in some genome editing approaches (Mertz et al., 2022; Rees and Liu, 2018; Chen and Liu, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mertz et al., 2022; Rees and Liu, 2018; Chen and Liu, 2023

claim: DNA mismatches, if unrepaired, are sources of genetic variation such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms and point mutations which can alter the cellular phenotype and cause dysfunction, diseases, and cancer.
source: DNA mismatches, if unrepaired, are sources of genetic variation such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms and point mutations which can alter the cellular phenotype and cause dysfunction, diseases, and cancer (Li, 2008; Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li, 2008; Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011

claim: DNA mismatches alter the physical properties of DNA such as local flexibility and conformational heterogeneity.
source: DNA mismatches also alter the physical properties of DNA such as local flexibility and conformational heterogeneity (Fields et al., 2013; Isaacs and Spielmann, 2004; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fields et al., 2013; Isaacs and Spielmann, 2004; Wang et al., 2003

claim: In eukaryotes, DNA is packaged into a basic unit, the nucleosome, which consists of 147 base pairs (bp) of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer core.
source: In eukaryotes, DNA is packaged into a basic unit, the nucleosome, which consists of 147 base pairs (bp) of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer core (Kornberg, 1974; Chen et al., 2021; Luger et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kornberg, 1974; Chen et al., 2021; Luger et al., 2012

claim: In vivo, nucleosomes are regularly arranged along DNA like 'beads on a string', with short linker DNA separating the beads.
source: In vivo, nucleosomes are regularly arranged along DNA like 'beads on a string', with short linker DNA separating the beads (Kornberg, 1974; Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kornberg, 1974; Chen et al., 2021

claim: The rate of genetic variation along the genome is correlated with nucleosome positions.
source: It has been commonly observed that the rate of genetic variation along the genome is correlated with nucleosome positions.
evidence: Supported by established scientific consensus

claim: The base substitution rate is higher nearer the center of a nucleosome and increases with increasing nucleosome occupancy.
source: Although not without an exception (Chen et al., 2012), studies have shown that the base substitution rate is higher nearer the center of a nucleosome and increases with increasing nucleosome occupancy (Semple and Taylor, 2009; Sasaki et al., 2009; Warnecke et al., 2008; Washietl et al., 2008; Sabarinathan et al., 2016; Tolstorukov et al., 2011; Hara et al., 2000; Yazdi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Semple and Taylor, 2009; Sasaki et al., 2009; Warnecke et al., 2008; Washietl et al., 2008; Sabarinathan et al., 2016; Tolstorukov et al., 2011; Hara et al., 2000; Yazdi et al., 2015

claim: One possible explanation for the correlation between base substitution rate and nucleosome position is that nucleosomes impose a barrier preventing the repair machinery from detecting and repairing a mismatch or a bulky DNA adduct induced by ultraviolet.
source: One possible explanation for this correlation is that nucleosomes impose a barrier preventing the repair machinery from detecting and repairing a mismatch (Li and Luscombe, 2020) or a bulky DNA adduct induced by ultraviolet (Sabarinathan et al., 2016), thus leading to substitutions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Li and Luscombe, 2020; Sabarinathan et al., 2016

claim: It is unknown how substrates for DNA repair such as mismatches and bulky adducts may affect nucleosome mechanical stability and nucleosomal DNA unwrapping.
source: Currently, it is unknown how substrates for DNA repair such as mismatches and bulky adducts may affect nucleosome mechanical stability and nucleosomal DNA unwrapping, which may affect accessibility of the nucleosomal DNA to the repair machinery.
evidence: Statement of unknown knowledge gap

claim: RNA polymerase II can initiate transcription at 4 pN of hindering force.
source: RNA polymerase II can initiate transcription at 4 pN of hindering force (Fazal et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fazal et al., 2015

claim: RNA polymerase II elongation activity continues until it stalls at ~10 pN of hindering force.
source: and its elongation activity continues until it stalls at ~10 pN of hindering force (Galburt et al., 2007; Schweikhard et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Galburt et al., 2007; Schweikhard et al., 2014

claim: Chromatin remodeling enzymes induce processive and directional sliding of single nucleosomes when the DNA is under ~5 pN of tension.
source: Another class of motor protein, chromatin remodeling enzymes, was also shown to induce processive and directional sliding of single nucleosomes when the DNA is under similar amount of tension (~5 pN; Kim et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2024

claim: There is a correlation between DNA flexibility and nucleosome stability under tension using the 601 nucleosome positioning sequence.
source: In an earlier work, we demonstrated a correlation between DNA flexibility and nucleosome stability under tension using the 601 nucleosome positioning sequence (Ngo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ngo et al., 2015

claim: The 601 DNA around the histone core can unwrap asymmetrically under tension.
source: We showed that the 601 DNA around the histone core can unwrap asymmetrically under tension.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ngo et al., 2015 in the same sentence context

claim: One side of the outer DNA turn unwraps at a lower force and the other side unwraps at a higher force.
source: One side of the outer DNA turn unwraps at a lower force and the other side unwraps at a higher force.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ngo et al., 2015 in the same sentence context

claim: The direction of asymmetry in nucleosome unwrapping is controlled by the relative DNA flexibility of the two DNA halves flanking the dyad.
source: The direction of asymmetry is controlled by the relative DNA flexibility of the two DNA halves flanking the dyad.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ngo et al., 2015 in the same sentence context

claim: Unwrapping force is lower for the nucleosomal DNA side with lower flexibility and vice versa.
source: Unwrapping force is lower for the nucleosomal DNA side with lower flexibility and vice versa.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ngo et al., 2015 in the same sentence context

claim: Cytosine modifications that make DNA more flexible made the nucleosome mechanically more stable and vice versa.
source: In addition, cytosine modifications that make DNA more flexible made the nucleosome mechanically more stable and vice versa (Ngo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ngo et al., 2016

claim: A single base-pair C-C mismatch enhances DNA bendability for the 601-nucleosome positioning sequence.
source: We found that a single base-pair C-C mismatch enhances DNA bendability and nucleosome mechanical stability for the 601-nucleosome positioning sequence.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from single-molecule DNA cyclization assay

claim: A single base-pair C-C mismatch enhances nucleosome mechanical stability for the 601-nucleosome positioning sequence.
source: We found that a single base-pair C-C mismatch enhances DNA bendability and nucleosome mechanical stability for the 601-nucleosome positioning sequence.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optical trap combined with single-molecule FRET

claim: An increase in force required for DNA unwrapping from the histone core is observed for single base-pair C-C mismatches placed at the inner turn, at the outer turn, or at the junction of the inner and outer turn of the nucleosome.
source: An increase in force required for DNA unwrapping from the histone core is observed for single base-pair C-C mismatches placed at three tested positions: at the inner turn, at the outer turn, or at the junction of the inner and outer turn of the nucleosome.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from fluorescence-force spectroscopy

claim: Nucleosomal DNA accessibility is reduced by mismatches, potentially explaining the preferred accumulation of single-nucleotide substitutions in the nucleosome core.
source: The results support a model where nucleosomal DNA accessibility is reduced by mismatches, potentially explaining the preferred accumulation of single-nucleotide substitutions in the nucleosome core and serving as the source of genetic variation during evolution and cancer progression.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on nucleosome mechanical stability

claim: Yeast nucleosomes are mechanically less stable than Xenopus nucleosomes.
source: Mechanical stability of an intact nucleosome, that is mismatch-free, is also dependent on the species as we find that yeast nucleosomes are mechanically less stable and more symmetrical in the outer turn unwrapping compared to Xenopus nucleosomes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing yeast and Xenopus nucleosomes

claim: Yeast nucleosomes are more symmetrical in the outer turn unwrapping compared to Xenopus nucleosomes.
source: Mechanical stability of an intact nucleosome, that is mismatch-free, is also dependent on the species as we find that yeast nucleosomes are mechanically less stable and more symmetrical in the outer turn unwrapping compared to Xenopus nucleosomes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing yeast and Xenopus nucleosomes

claim: All four DNA constructs (601, 601-R18, 601-R39, and 601-R56) yielded nucleosomes with the same electrophoretic mobility.
source: All four DNA constructs (601, 601-R18, 601-R39, and 601-R56) yielded nucleosomes with the same electrophoretic mobility and single-molecule FRET value, indicating that the nucleosomes are homogeneously positioned for all four constructs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: All four DNA constructs (601, 601-R18, 601-R39, and 601-R56) yielded nucleosomes with the same single-molecule FRET value.
source: All four DNA constructs (601, 601-R18, 601-R39, and 601-R56) yielded nucleosomes with the same electrophoretic mobility and single-molecule FRET value, indicating that the nucleosomes are homogeneously positioned for all four constructs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: A single mismatch (A-A or T-T) does not affect the nucleosome position.
source: This is consistent with a previous single-nucleotide resolution mapping of dyad position from of a library of mismatches in all possible positions along the 601 sequence or a budding yeast native sequence which showed that a single mismatch (A-A or T-T) does not affect the nucleosome position (Park et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Park et al., 2023

claim: Mismatch-containing nucleosomes showed different behaviors between stretching cycles.
source: However, under perturbation by force, although unmodified nucleosomes showed the same behavior between stretching cycles (Ngo et al., 2015), mismatch-containing nucleosomes showed different behaviors between stretching cycles (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: The ED1 side of the mismatch containing nucleosomes unwrapped at lower forces for the first few cycles and then at higher forces for subsequent cycles.
source: The ED1 side of the mismatch containing nucleosomes unwrapped at lower forces for the first few cycles and then at higher forces for subsequent cycles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from fluorescence-force spectroscopy

claim: After relaxation, there is a general trend of an increase in unwrapping force in the subsequent stretching cycles for mismatch-containing nucleosomes.
source: After relaxation, we observed a general trend of an increase in unwrapping force in the subsequent stretching cycles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from fluorescence-force spectroscopy

claim: The force range where FRET reduced gradually accompanied by fluctuations was wider and extended to higher force for mismatch-containing nucleosomes compared to 601 nucleosomes.
source: However, the force range where FRET reduced gradually accompanied by fluctuations was wider and extended to higher force for mismatch-containing nucleosomes (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E

claim: The averaged FRET vs. force pattern for 601-R39 showed an increase in unwrapping force for the mismatch-containing nucleosomes.
source: The averaged FRET vs. force pattern for 601-R39 showed an increase in unwrapping force for the mismatch-containing nucleosomes (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The increase in unwrapping force for all three mismatch containing constructs indicates that local flexibility of either the inner turn or the outer turn regulates nucleosome unwrapping.
source: The increase in unwrapping force for all three mismatch containing constructs indicates that local flexibility of either the inner turn or the outer turn regulates nucleosome unwrapping (Figure 4).
evidence: Inference from experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: The mismatch construct 601-R39 with ED2 labeling yielded nearly the same unwrapping pattern as the 601 nucleosome.
source: The mismatch construct yielded nearly the same unwrapping pattern as the 601 nucleosome, suggesting the change in local flexibility induced by the mismatch has a strengthening effect against unwrapping only for the side containing the mismatch (the ED1 side).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from fluorescence-force spectroscopy with ED2 labeling

claim: The change in local flexibility induced by the mismatch has a strengthening effect against unwrapping only for the side containing the mismatch.
source: The mismatch construct yielded nearly the same unwrapping pattern as the 601 nucleosome, suggesting the change in local flexibility induced by the mismatch has a strengthening effect against unwrapping only for the side containing the mismatch (the ED1 side).
evidence: Inference from experimental data comparing ED1 and ED2 sides

claim: C-C is one of the most flexible mismatches.
source: A previous study using a DNA buckling assay suggested that C-C is one of the most flexible mismatches (Fields et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fields et al., 2013

claim: The mismatch induced a ~sevenfold increase in the rate of DNA cyclization of the TA-poor side.
source: Indeed, the mismatch induced a~ sevenfold increase in the rate of DNA cyclization of the TA-poor side.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from DNA cyclization assay

claim: Adding a C-C mismatch reduced the looping time from 57 min to 32 min (601-R18-RH), 9 min (601-R39-RH), and 32 min (601-R56-RH).
source: Adding a C-C mismatch reduced the looping time from 57 min to 32 min (601-R18-RH), 9 min (601-R39-RH), and 32 min (601-R56-RH).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from DNA cyclization assay shown in Figure 5B

claim: The reduction in apparent looping time was larger with the mismatch placing at the center (601-R39-RH) than toward the side of the RH fragment (601-R18-RH,601-R56-RH).
source: The reduction in apparent looping time was larger with the mismatch placing at the center (601-R39-RH) than toward the side of the RH fragment (601-R18-RH,601-R56-RH) likely because the looping measurement is more sensitive to the change in flexibility at the center of the DNA fragment.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from DNA cyclization assay with inference about measurement sensitivity

claim: The cyclizability of surface-tethered DNA constructs possesses an oscillatory dependence on the position of the biotin tether.
source: The cyclizability of surface-tethered DNA constructs was shown to possess an oscillatory dependence on the position of the biotin tether (Basu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Basu et al., 2021

claim: Moving the location of the biotin tether by half the helical repeat (~5 bp) can lead to a large change in cyclization rate.
source: For example, moving the location of the biotin tether by half the helical repeat (~5 bp) can lead to a large change in cyclization rate (Basu et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Basu et al., 2021

claim: The overall looping rates of both the 601-RH-16 and 601-R18-RH-16 constructs were higher than those for the 601-RH and 601-R18-RH constructs.
source: We found that the overall looping rates of both the 601-RH-16 and 601-R18-RH-16 constructs were higher than those for the 601-RH and 601-R18-RH constructs, indicating that moving the biotin tether towards the center of the molecule increases looping rate (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The 601-R18-RH-16 construct, which contains a mismatch, looped faster than the 601-RH-16 construct without a mismatch.
source: However, the 601-R18-RH-16 construct, which contains a mismatch, still looped faster than the 601-RH-16 construct without a mismatch (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The presence of the C-C mismatch makes the construct loop faster.
source: We thus conclude that the presence of the C-C mismatch makes the construct loop faster, and that this is not an artifact specific to the biotin tether location.
evidence: Inference from experimental data comparing constructs with different biotin positions

claim: Significant reduction in looping time compared to the intact DNA control was observed for all mismatch types except G-containing mismatches (G-G, G-T and G-A mismatches).
source: We observed significant reduction in looping time compared to the intact DNA control (no mismatch) with the exception of G-containing mismatches (G-G, G-T and G-A mismatches).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from DNA cyclization assay shown in Figure 6

claim: The C-containing mismatches (C-C, C-A and C-T) showed the largest reduction in looping times, suggesting that they make DNA most bendable.
source: The C-containing mismatches (C-C, C-A and C-T) showed the largest reduction in looping times, suggesting that they make DNA most bendable.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on looping times shown in Figure 6

claim: Outer turn FRET probes on both sides ED1 and ED2 displayed slightly lower zero-force FRET values for yeast nucleosomes compared to Xenopus nucleosomes.
source: Outer turn FRET probes on both sides ED1 and ED2 displayed slightly lower zero-force FRET values for yeast nucleosomes compared to Xenopus nucleosomes (Figure 7)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7

claim: The DNA entry/exit may be more loosely bound on histone core for yeast nucleosomes compared to Xenopus nucleosomes.
source: Outer turn FRET probes on both sides ED1 and ED2 displayed slightly lower zero-force FRET values for yeast nucleosomes compared to Xenopus nucleosomes (Figure 7), indicating that the DNA entry/exit may be more loosely bound on histone core for yeast nucleosomes.
evidence: Inference from experimental FRET data shown in Figure 7

claim: The inner turn FRET probe showed similar zero-force FRET values for yeast and Xenopus nucleosomes.
source: In contrast, the inner turn FRET probe showed similar zero-force FRET values for yeast and Xenopus nucleosomes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from fluorescence-force spectroscopy

claim: The strong side probe ED2 showed lower mechanical stability for yeast histones, with 40% of the molecules having unwrapping force of lower than 5 pN and the other 60% of the molecules being unwrapped by a force between 5 and 15 pN.
source: With pulling force applied, the stretching pattern for ED1 is similar for both nucleosomes while the strong side probe ED2 showed lower mechanical stability for yeast histones, with 40% of the molecules having unwrapping force of lower than 5 pN and the other 60% of the molecules being unwrapped by a force between 5 and 15 pN (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B

claim: The inner turn probe showed a stepwise unwrapping pattern with initial FRET reduction at less than 5 pN followed by stable FRET and a final unwrapping at a force higher than 20 pN.
source: The inner turn probe showed a stepwise unwrapping pattern with initial FRET reduction at less than 5 pN followed by stable FRET and a final unwrapping at a force higher than 20 pN (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Nucleosomes made with yeast histones are mechanically less stable, and unwrap less asymmetrically than nucleosomes made with Xenopus histones.
source: These observations for both outer turn and inner turn probes suggested that nucleosomes made with yeast histones are mechanically less stable, and unwrap less asymmetrically than nucleosomes made with Xenopus histones.
evidence: Inference from experimental data comparing yeast and Xenopus nucleosomes

claim: The crystal structure of the yeast nucleosome suggests that yeast nucleosome architecture is subtly destabilized in comparison with nucleosomes from higher eukaryotes.
source: The crystal structure of the yeast nucleosome suggests that yeast nucleosome architecture is subtly destabilized in comparison with nucleosomes from higher eukaryotes (White et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 2001

claim: Yeast histone protein sequences are not well conserved relative to vertebrate histones (H2A, 77%; H2B, 73%; H3, 90%; H4, 92% identities).
source: Yeast histone protein sequences are not well conserved relative to vertebrate histones (H2A, 77%; H2B, 73%; H3, 90%; H4, 92% identities), and this divergence likely contributes to differences in nucleosome stability.
evidence: Established knowledge about histone sequence conservation

claim: Substitution of three residues in yeast H3 α3-helix (Q120, K121, K125) with corresponding human H3.1/H3.3 residues (QK…K replaced with MP…Q) caused severe growth defects, elevated nuclease sensitivity, reduced nucleosome positioning and nucleosome relocation to preferred locations predicted by DNA sequence alone.
source: Substitution of three residues in yeast H3 α3-helix (Q120, K121, K125) very near the nucleosome dyad with corresponding human H3.1/H3.3 residues (QK…K replaced with MP…Q) caused severe growth defects, elevated nuclease sensitivity, reduced nucleosome positioning and nucleosome relocation to preferred locations predicted by DNA sequence alone (McBurney et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to McBurney et al., 2016

claim: The yeast histone octamer harboring wild type H3 may be less capable of wrapping DNA over the histone core, leading to reduced resistance to the unwrapping force for the more flexible half of the 601 positioning sequence.
source: The yeast histone octamer harboring wild type H3 may be less capable of wrapping DNA over the histone core, leading to reduced resistance to the unwrapping force for the more flexible half of the 601positioning sequence.
evidence: Inference from experimental data and structural knowledge

claim: How DNA mechanics, determined by sequence, chemical modifications and mismatches, is translated to nucleosome mechanics may be dependent on species-specific differences in histone sequence and post-translation modifications.
source: Overall, our data suggest that how DNA mechanics, determined by sequence (Ngo et al., 2015; Basu et al., 2021; Basu et al., 2022), chemical modifications (Ngo et al., 2016) and mismatches (Vafabakhsh and Ha, 2012; Jeong and Kim, 2019), is translated to nucleosome mechanics may be dependent on species-specific differences in histone sequence and post-translation modifications, which need to be examined in future studies.
evidence: Inference from experimental data with citations to supporting studies

claim: The artificial 601 sequence does not preferentially or strongly position the nucleosomes in vivo as expected.
source: Previous studies have showed that the artificial 601 sequence do not preferentially or strongly position the nucleosomes in vivo as expected (Lancrey et al., 2022; Perales et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lancrey et al., 2022; Perales et al., 2011

claim: A native sequence from the yeast gene SWH1 forms a nucleosome in vitro centered at the dyad position in vivo.
source: We recently reported a native sequence from the yeast gene SWH1 that forms a nucleosome in vitro centered at the dyad position in vivo (Park et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Park et al., 2023

claim: The enhancement of the mechanical stability of the nucleosome can potentially lead to the nucleosome's decreased accessibility for the mismatch repair mechanism, which can account for the accumulation of single-nucleotide polymorphisms near the nucleosome dyad.
source: While the enhancement of the mechanical stability of the nucleosome can potentially lead to the nucleosome's decreased accessibility for the mismatch repair mechanism, which can account for the accumulation of single-nucleotide polymorphisms near the nucleosome dyad, other functional implications of the enhanced mechanical stability cannot be precluded.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings

claim: Enhanced mechanical stability might shield DNA from transcription, which prevents the expression of genes that contain misincorporated nucleotides.
source: For example, enhanced mechanical stability might shield DNA from transcription, which prevents the expression of genes that contain misincorporated nucleotides.
evidence: Speculation about potential functional implications

claim: A DNA mismatch can increase DNA bendability.
source: Using the looping time of single-molecule DNA cyclization as a measure of DNA bendability, we showed that a DNA mismatch can increase DNA bendability.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from single-molecule DNA cyclization assay

claim: The enhancement of DNA flexibility by mismatches may be explained by the existence of a kink at the mismatch position on the DNA.
source: A possible explanation for the enhancement of DNA flexibility is the existence of a kink at the mismatch position on the DNA.
evidence: Speculation about mechanism

claim: The enhancement of mechanical stability of nucleosomes reconstituted from mismatch-containing DNA constructs was observed.
source: We observed the enhancement of mechanical stability of nucleosomes reconstituted from mismatch-containing DNA constructs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from fluorescence-force spectroscopy

claim: The findings are in broad agreement with previous studies that showed positive correlation between DNA flexibility and nucleosome mechanical stability when DNA sequences or cytosine methylation was altered.
source: A defect making the system more stable may appear counterintuitive but given that the same mismatch can make DNA more flexible, our findings are in broad agreements with previous studies that showed positive correlation between DNA flexibility and nucleosome mechanical stability when DNA sequences or cytosine methylation was altered (Ngo et al., 2015; Ngo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ngo et al., 2015; Ngo et al., 2016

claim: The 601 positioning sequence has TA-rich side that has four TA dinucleotides spaced with 10 bp periodicity and is more flexible than the TA-poor side.
source: The 601 positioning sequence has TA-rich side that has four TA dinucleotides spaced with 10 bp periodicity and is more flexible than the TA-poor side (Ngo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ngo et al., 2015

claim: The 601 nucleosome is more stable on the TA-rich side.
source: The 601 nucleosome is more stable on the TA-rich side (Ngo et al., 2015; Díaz-Celis et al., 2022; Tokuda et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Ngo et al., 2015; Díaz-Celis et al., 2022; Tokuda et al., 2018

claim: A single mismatch in the TA-poor side can symmetrize DNA flexibility of the 601 nucleosome.
source: This increase in DNA flexibility matches the ~sevenfold larger cyclization rate of the TA-rich side compared to the TA-poor side (Ngo et al., 2015), suggesting that a single mismatch in the TA-poor side can symmetrize DNA flexibility of the 601 nucleosome.
evidence: Inference from experimental data comparing cyclization rates

claim: When the flexibility symmetry was obtained via a mismatch in the TA-poor side, the TA-rich side remained mechanically stable, unwrapping at only high forces.
source: However, unlike flexibility symmetry achieved by TA repeats where which side unwraps at low forces became stochastic (Ngo et al., 2015), when the flexibility symmetry was obtained via a mismatch in the TA-poor side, the TA-rich side remained mechanically stable, unwrapping at only high forces.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from fluorescence-force spectroscopy

claim: Although the apparent flexibility is similar between DNA containing a mismatch vs a flexible sequence element, the mismatch does not have a global effect on the coordination of unwrapping of the two DNA ends.
source: This difference suggests that although the apparent flexibility is similar between DNA containing a mismatch vs a flexible sequence element, the mismatch does not have a global effect on the coordination of unwrapping of the two DNA ends.
evidence: Inference from experimental data comparing different flexibility mechanisms

claim: The enhanced nucleosome mechanical stability suggests that a mismatch will reduce nucleosomal DNA accessibility.
source: The enhanced nucleosome mechanical stability we observed suggests that a mismatch will reduce nucleosomal DNA accessibility.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on mechanical stability

claim: The reduction in nucleosomal DNA accessibility would hinder the activity of the DNA mismatch repair machinery on nucleosomal DNA.
source: The reduction in nucleosomal DNA accessibility would hinder the activity of the DNA mismatch repair machinery on nucleosomal DNA.
evidence: Inference from reduced accessibility

claim: An unrepaired mismatch leads to a point mutation which may be the source for genetic variation during evolution and cancer progression.
source: An unrepaired mismatch leads to a point mutation which may be the source for genetic variation during evolution and cancer progression.
evidence: Established knowledge about consequences of unrepaired mismatches

claim: The frequency of single-nucleotide polymorphism is higher near the nucleosome dyad for nucleosomes that are strongly positioned in vivo.
source: In fact, previous observations showed that the frequency of single-nucleotide polymorphism is higher near the nucleosome dyad for nucleosomes that are strongly positioned in vivo (Li and Luscombe, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li and Luscombe, 2020

claim: The higher frequency of substitutions in the nucleosomal DNA may be attributed to the difficulty of accessing the extra-stable nucleosomes.
source: The higher frequency of substitutions in the nucleosomal DNA may be attributed to the difficulty of accessing the extra-stable nucleosomes.
evidence: Inference connecting experimental findings to observed substitution patterns

claim: Even without an enhanced stability, a mismatch within a nucleosome would be more difficult to detect for mismatch repair machineries compared to a mismatch in a non-nucleosomal DNA.
source: We also note that even without an enhanced stability, a mismatch within a nucleosome would be more difficult to detect for mismatch repair machineries compared to a mismatch in a non-nucleosomal DNA.
evidence: Inference based on nucleosome structure

claim: Most of nascent mismatches may be detected for repair before nucleosome deposition because mismatch repair machineries accompany the replisome.
source: Because mismatch repair machineries accompany the replisome, most of nascent mismatches may be detected for repair before nucleosome deposition.
evidence: Inference based on knowledge of repair machinery timing

claim: The decrease in accessibility predicted based on the data may be important only in rare cases a mismatch is not detected prior to the deposition of a nucleosome on the nascent DNA or in cases where a mismatch is generated via a non-replicative mechanism.
source: Therefore, the decrease in accessibility predicted based on our data here may be important only in rare cases a mismatch is not detected prior to the deposition of a nucleosome on the nascent DNA or in cases where a mismatch is generated via a non-replicative mechanism.
evidence: Inference about when the findings would be relevant

claim: If more flexible elements in the DNA make a nucleosome mechanically stronger, other mismatches, DNA lesions and alternative DNA structures such as DNA single strand damages, bulky adducts and R-loops that alter DNA local flexibility would also change nucleosome mechanical stability accordingly.
source: If indeed more flexible elements in the DNA make a nucleosome mechanically stronger, as shown here for the C-C mismatch and previously for different sequences and cytosine modifications (Ngo et al., 2015; Ngo et al., 2016), we can predict that other mismatches, DNA lesions and alternative DNA structures such as DNA single strand damages, bulky adducts and R-loops (Huang and Zhou, 2021) that alter DNA local flexibility would also change nucleosome mechanical stability accordingly.
evidence: Prediction based on experimental findings and citations
